To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the rate of change in our society exceeds the rate at which dependable, generalizable findings emerge from relevant developmental research.

(1) the rate of societal change has exceeded the rate of progress in our understanding of the processes that produce that change, and (2) the research establishment in developmental research, while it has produced some excellent results, is not producing them fast enough.

(1) the pace at which the scientific community produces dependable, agreed upon results is slower than the pace at which society changes; and that (2) the research establishment in developmental research is not functioning at an optimal level.

the processes by which human behavior develops.
the question of how to achieve a more rapid rate of progress through the development of more comparable and more generalizable findings in the field of developmental psychology.
the development of children, yet we are still in the developmental stage ourselves.

the research establishment in developmental science, as in other fields, is not as effective as it could be, that the system is capable of self-correction, and that it can be improved.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pace of change in our society has outstripped the pace of change among developmental psychologists.
we have found the research establishment in developmental science to be in need of some changes that will enable it to respond more effectively to the challenge of rapid societal change.
we need to do better and faster.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be more open to change.
we need to be more aware of the context of the research we are doing and how that context can impact our results.

we need a new approach to developmental research, one that is based on a new understanding of the nature of developmental science, and one that takes into consideration the nature of developmental phenomena.
